c5e3c1fa-75e8-46ff-9ee8-26a394a70501.recap: The piece argues the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations shows households now assign a 44.4% probability to unemployment rising over the next year, the highest since April 2020, alongside pessimism about finding a new job if laid off. This anxiety is showing up in behavior: existing home sales fell below a 4-million annualized pace in August even as inventory hit its highest level since 2019 (4.9 months' supply, most in over a decade), suggesting weak demand rather than supply shortage is now the constraint. Consumer credit grew $15 billion in July, the most in three years, but almost entirely via non-revolving credit (autos, student loans) possibly pulled forward on fear of future financing costs, while revolving (credit card) credit rose just $2.8 billion, indicating caution on open-ended borrowing. Despite expecting necessities (gas, food, rent, medical, college) to get pricier, households' median 1-year inflation expectation fell for a third straight month to 3.58%, with 3-year at 3.2% and 5-year steady at 3%. The host ties this to the bond market: nominal yields are rising but the curve remains historically flat and breakevens benign, which he argues is inconsistent with markets pricing a genuine inflation spiral, and more consistent with front-end pressure from expected prolonged Fed hawkishness plus seasonal September effects. The overall argument is that an energy/necessities price shock is colliding with a deteriorating, "no hire" labor market to produce disinflationary demand destruction, and that the Fed's hawkish stance is unsupported by its own data.

fecd7090-ad46-11f1-b991-7f70ab8e99f7.recap: Hosts of Blockworks' Forward Guidance discuss Treasury Secretary Bessent's push to be seen as controlling bond markets: Japan's MOF raised its long-JGB buyback plan from an initially guided $4bn minimum to $6bn, yet long JGB yields still rose, which the hosts read as the bond market calling his bluff, even as yen intervention (from ~160 down to ~153) has worked better. A regression of the 10-year UST yield against nominal GDP implies a 'fair value' around 5.8% if 6.6% nominal GDP growth persists. They then dissect the August PPI print: headline +0.4% m/m in line with consensus, core actually softer than expected at +0.2%, with the hot part driven by energy/transport pass-through (rising diesel) while items feeding into PCE, like portfolio services (-1.6%), were benign — yet markets reacted aggressively, pushing hike odds from roughly 50/50 to about 70% for next week's FOMC. They discuss the risk of hiking into an oil supply shock (historically reversed within a year and recessionary), Waller's data-dependent, single-print reaction function, and SOFR pricing roughly three hikes into mid-2026, which they view as unlikely to be delivered given decelerating growth and disinflationary demand destruction from $100+ oil. A proprietary study suggests that when long-end selloffs are term-premium-led (as now) rather than inflation-expectation-led (as in 2022), a first 'credibility' hike tends to be followed by long yields falling. They close discussing the 'debasement trade' pullback as tactical noise within an intact longer-term thesis, and fading sentiment in AI/semiconductor trades amid political backlash and unwind of leveraged positioning.
terms: PPI -- Producer Price Index, measuring prices received by producers for output
PCE -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
term premium -- the extra yield investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds beyond expected short-rate path
FOMC -- Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's rate-setting body
SOFR curve -- market-implied path of the Secured Overnight Financing Rate used to gauge expected Fed policy
